reference:
A Community Air-Quality Project

Last spring, the Greenfield Community Centre started a small air-quality project. The centre is near a busy road and a new building site. Many families wanted to know if the air was safe for children. The project leader, Ms. Chen, said, "We cannot test every street, so we must choose our methods carefully." The team compared three ways to monitor air quality: low-cost sensors, official monitoring stations, and simple dust traps. Low-cost sensors are small boxes that people can put on a balcony or a window. They are cheap, and they send data every minute. However, because they are cheap, they may not be very accurate. Ms. Chen explained, "The sensor is useful for showing changes during the day, but it might give a wrong number when the air is very wet." The team decided to use sensors in ten homes near the road.

Part 1
Do you often check the air quality in your city?
What do you do when the air is bad?
Do you prefer to walk or take a bus? Why?
Is there a park near your home?

Part 2
Describe a time when you compared two ways to do something. You should say: what you compared; why you compared them; what the result was; and explain what you learned from the comparison.

Part 3
Why might people use cheap sensors instead of official stations?
What can governments do to improve air quality?
Do you think people can take action even without perfect data?
How might technology change environmental monitoring in the future?
